front: State the four anatomic components of tetralogy of Fallot.
back: 1) Large perimembranous VSD (unrestrictive). 2) Overriding aorta over the septum. 3) Right ventricular outflow tract obstruction (typically infundibular + valvular PS). 4) Right ventricular hypertrophy (consequence).

front: How is a hypercyanotic 'tet spell' managed acutely?
back: Knee-chest position (increases SVR → reduces R-to-L shunt), oxygen, fluid bolus, morphine, phenylephrine (α-agonist to raise SVR), and propranolol (decreases infundibular spasm).

front: What is the most common valvular complication after TOF repair, and how is it managed long-term?
back: Chronic free pulmonary regurgitation from a transannular RVOT patch. RV dilation progresses; pulmonary valve replacement (surgical or percutaneous) is often needed.

front: In d-TGA, from which ventricle does each great artery arise?
back: Aorta arises from the RIGHT ventricle. Pulmonary artery arises from the LEFT ventricle. This creates parallel circulations incompatible with life without mixing (PDA, PFO, VSD).

front: Which repair is now standard for simple d-TGA and when is it performed?
back: Arterial switch operation (Jatene, 1976) — great arteries switched at the level of the sinotubular junction with coronary reimplantation. Typically performed in the neonatal period (first 2 weeks of life).

front: Late complications of the arterial switch operation for d-TGA?
back: Neo-aortic root dilation, neo-aortic valve regurgitation, coronary ostial stenosis, branch pulmonary artery stenosis.

front: Long-term problems after a Mustard or Senning atrial-switch operation for d-TGA?
back: The morphologic RV remains the systemic ventricle → late RV failure, systemic AV (tricuspid) valve regurgitation, sinus node dysfunction, atrial arrhythmias, and baffle stenosis or leaks.

front: Describe the Rastelli procedure and its indications.
back: For d-TGA + VSD + LV outflow obstruction (PS). LV output is baffled through the VSD to the aorta; an RV-to-PA conduit is placed.

front: Explain 'double discordance' in congenitally corrected TGA (cctga / L-TGA).
back: AV discordance (RA connects to morphologic LV, LA connects to morphologic RV) AND VA discordance (morphologic LV connects to PA, morphologic RV connects to aorta). Blood flow is physiologically normal, but the morphologic RV serves as the systemic ventricle.

front: What are the major long-term problems with cctga?
back: Progressive failure of the systemic morphologic RV, systemic AV valve regurgitation (often Ebstein-like tricuspid valve), and complete heart block (rate ~2%/year).

front: Name the three main types of AV canal defect.
back: Partial (primum ASD + cleft AMVL only). Transitional (primum ASD + inlet VSD but two separate AV valves). Complete (primum ASD + inlet VSD + common AV valve).

front: Which congenital lesion is most classically associated with Down syndrome?
back: Complete atrioventricular canal defect (AVSD).

front: Truncus arteriosus — describe the basic anatomy.
back: Single common arterial trunk arises from both ventricles (astride a large subarterial VSD) and gives rise to the coronary arteries, pulmonary arteries, and aorta. The truncal valve (bicuspid or quadricuspid) is often abnormal — insufficiency is common.

front: Classic echo triad of tricuspid atresia?
back: 1) No visible tricuspid valve — a solid tissue band replaces it. 2) Small, hypoplastic RV. 3) Obligate atrial-level right-to-left shunt (ASD or PFO). A VSD or PDA usually supplies pulmonary flow.

front: State the key echo criteria for Ebstein's anomaly.
back: Apical displacement of the septal tricuspid leaflet > 8 mm/m² BSA (or > 20 mm absolute); atrialization of the proximal RV; redundant sail-like anterior TV leaflet. Often with PFO/ASD and right-to-left shunting.

front: What percentage of Ebstein's anomaly patients have Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome?
back: ~25%. The accessory pathway is located on the tricuspid annulus.

front: State the goals of the Fontan operation.
back: 1) Separate systemic and pulmonary circulations. 2) Remove volume load from the single functional ventricle. 3) Direct systemic venous blood passively to the pulmonary arteries (no pumping chamber in the pulmonary circuit).

front: List three prerequisites for a successful Fontan operation.
back: Low pulmonary vascular resistance, preserved single-ventricular function, and unobstructed pulmonary artery anatomy. High PVR predicts Fontan failure.

front: Give three late complications of the Fontan operation.
back: Protein-losing enteropathy, plastic bronchitis, Fontan-associated liver disease, atrial arrhythmias, thromboembolism, and systemic AV valve regurgitation.

front: List the four anatomic types of TAPVR and their approximate frequencies.
back: Supracardiac (~45%) via vertical vein to innominate. Cardiac (~26%) to coronary sinus. Infracardiac (~24%) through diaphragm to portal/hepatic system — usually obstructed. Mixed (~5%).

front: Which type of TAPVR is a surgical emergency?
back: Infracardiac (infradiaphragmatic) TAPVR — the anomalous veins pass through the diaphragm and are almost invariably obstructed as they course through the liver.

front: Echo features of TAPVR?
back: Large right ventricle, small left heart, right-to-left atrial-level shunt (ASD is always present), and possibly complex ventricular anatomy (single ventricle).
